Śāstā
(‘one who commands’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu genius has the peculiar virtue of reconciling the irreconcilables. At a time when the Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas were at loggerheads, the story in the Bhāgavata (8.12), of शिव being enraptured by the voluptuous beauty of (Viṣṇu as) मोहिनी, the enchantress, must have come in very handy. By taking it to the logical conclusion it produced the wonderful deity Hariharaputra or शास्ता, more commonly known as ‘Ayyappan’ (a corrupted form of Ārya). Whatever he might have been in the beginning, he was certainly not a compromise candidate tolerated by both the groups, but Supreme God Himself, highly venerated by both.
Śabarīmalai AyyappaMythological accounts, of course, have their own story to tell. After the death of महिषासुर at the hands of दुर्गा, his spouse Mahiṣī performed severe austerities to please ब्रह्मा. She succeeded in getting the boon that she could not be killed by शिव or विष्णु. This newfound strength of Mahiṣī posed a formidable challenge to the gods and the world. शिव and विष्णु, who could not singly vanquish her, hit upon the plan of coming together as parents to create her destroyer. The child thus created was found by king Rājaśekhara of Panthalam in Kerala who named it as मणिकण्ठन् and brought it up as his own son, since he had no offspring. When मणिकण्ठन् was twelve years old, he killed Mahiṣī and brought leopardesses to his ड़थेर्’s palace since their milk was needed to cure the ‘headache’ of the queen. Meanwhile, the secret of मणिकण्ठन् being God Himself, had been revealed to the king. Adored by the king मणिकण्ठन् disappeared, after instructing him to build a temple at the place where his arrow would land. That was the summit of the hill शबरीमलै. The temple is said to have been built by विश्वकर्म and the image prepared and installed by परशुराम. The place attracts millions of pilgrims even now.
The word ‘Śāstā’ means one who controls and rules over the whole world. Mahāśāstā and Dharmaśāstā are the other names by which the deity is known. ‘Śāstā’ is one of the names of बुद्ध. The deity is said to ride on a white elephant called योगि. He is also described as the protector of धर्म. Hence some scholars opine that धर्म-शास्ता may be बुद्ध absorbed into the Hindu pantheon by the South Indian Hindus.
The image of शास्ता has four arms, three eyes and a peaceful countenance, and is seated in पद्मासन. Two of the hands carry the sword and the shield and the other two exhibit the Abhaya and Varada Mudrās.
According to another version, the image should have only two hands and two eyes, and should be seated with the legs folded. It should be bedecked with ornaments and have the यज्ञोपवीत. A crooked stick, fruits and tender leaves of plants are sometimes shown in his hands. A Vajradaṇḍa is also shown occasionally.
Images in the standing posture are also seen to exist, though rare.
The ritual पिल्ग्रिमगे to the shrine of Śrī अय्यप्पन् at शबरीमलै is considered to be extremely auspicious and meritorious. The पिल्ग्रिमगे itself has to be preceded by forty-one days of austerity during which period strict celibacy is to be observed as also restrictions regarding ड़ोओद्, speech and sleep.

Ṣaṣṭhī
(‘sixth aspect [of the Divine मोथेर्]’)
------------------------------------------
Ṣaṣṭhī is a minor goddess, the sixth among the sixteen mātṛkās (minor goddesses). She guards a newborn baby on the sixth day of its birth and also on the twenty-first day. She is worshipped in the delivery room itself.
She is the deity who can cause or cure the maladies of children.
Sometimes she is identified with देवसेना, the spouse of स्कन्द or Subrah-maṇya, and is worshipped along with him on the Skandaṣaṣṭhī day.

ṣaṣṭyabdapūrti-śānti
------------------------------------------
Known also as उग्ररथशान्ति, it is a propitiatory rite performed on the completion of 60 years in a man’s life. See ŚĀNTIS for details.

śastra
(‘that by which one is hurt’)
------------------------------------------
The words astra and शस्त्र are commonly used in the epics and the पुराणस्.
An astra is a missile discharged from a suitable instrument (like a bow) whereas a शस्त्र is a weapon (like a sword) which is directly wielded by the hand.
The word may also be used to indicate an instrument used in surgery.
In the वेदस् a शस्त्र refers to a laudatory hymn—used in a sacrifice—that is simply recited and not sung. A स्तोत्र is always sung.
A शस्त्र belongs to and follows a स्तोत्र.
Composed of several verses it is generally recited by the होतृ and his associates called śrotrakas. This recitation involves other steps like आहाव (summoning), प्रतिगर (response), tūṣṇīṁjapa (silent or inaudible recitation) and so on.

Ṣaṣṭitantra
(‘science of sixty topics’)
------------------------------------------
The Sāṅkhyadarśana is one of the oldest systems of Hindu philosophy whose origins can be traced even to the उपनिषद्स्.
The Ahirbudhnya Saṁhitā (12.19-30) refers to an ancient work on the Sāṅkhya known as the Ṣaṣṭitantra. Whether it was one particular ancient work or referred in general to any work (or works) of Śāṅkhya philosophy dealing with sixty topics, is difficult to say.
According to one version, Pañcaśikha—the third of the three original teachers of Sāṅkhya—is said to have composed this work.
The work is divided into two parts: The prākṛtamaṇḍala (with 32 subdivisions) and the vaikṛtamaṇḍala (with 28 sub-divisions).
The following is a general overview of the topics dealt with: प्रकृति; puruṣas; relation of the प्रकृति with the puruṣas; evolution of the categories from the प्रकृति; inactivity of the puruṣas; five viparyayas or misconceptions; nine tuṣṭis or contentments; twenty-eight kinds of defects of organs and eight सिद्धिस् or attainments.
It is believed that the Sāṅkhya of कपिल and आसुरि was theistic whereas पञ्चशिख made it atheistic.

Śāstrasiddhāntaleśasaṅgraha
------------------------------------------
This is a well-known and popular work of अप्पय्य दीक्षित (A.

-1592) (See APPAYYA DĪKṢITA for details.).
Also known as Siddhāntaleśa-saṅgraha, it is a comprehensive survey of the doctrinal interpretations and arguments as formulated by post-शङ्कर advaitins. Though called a ‘saṅgraha’ (an epitomised version) it is quite exhaustive.
There are four paricchedas or chapters. A very brief summary of the contents may be attempted as follows:
First Pariccheda
Nature of ब्रह्मन्; distinction between ईश्वर and jīvas; problem of causality of the world; nature and locus of अविद्या and māyā; nature and scope of विधि (injunction) in respect of Vedāntic study.
Second Pariccheda
Relative importance of Śruti (the scripture) and प्रत्यक्ष (direct perception); authority of the Śruti is to be accepted; nature of स्वप्न or dream and भ्रम or erroneous चोग्नितिओन्; the दृष्टि-सृष्टि-वाद; refutation of the theories that a जीव (individual सोउल्) is aṇu (atomic in size) and is different from ब्रह्मन्.
Third Pariccheda
Means of मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्; utility of कर्म or duties; the need for सṁन्यास or monastic life; discussion about mūlā-ज्ञान (root-nescience).
Fourth Pariccheda
On जीवन्मुक्ति; dispelling of अविद्या or इग्नोरन्चे; permanence of मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्; nature of लिबेरतिओन् in the context of एकजीववाद and anekajīvavāda.
The work has an excellent commentary—the Kṛṣṇālaṅkāra—by Acyutakṛṣṇā-नन्द Tīrtha.
See also ADVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA, DṚṢṬI-सृष्टि-VĀDA and EKAJĪVAVĀDA.
